SNATCHER CAUGHT.

PORTUGUESE LADY
ROBBED
ACCUSED SHIVERS IN COURT.

An elderly Chinese, describing himself as a shop employee, was smartly caught by European Sergeant Pointz just as the man was disappearing down a side street after a chase of 40 yards along Queen's Road Central. The reason for the hurried flight was that the man had purloined a Portuguese lady's handbag.

While out shopping in Queen's Road, Miss Amelia Maria Remedios, of No. 18, Jordan Road, Kowloon, noticed the man walking behind her and eyeing her handbag suspiciously. With his limping gait he was thought to be a beggar and no notice was taken of him. Seizing his opportunity the man snatched the handbag and ran away with it, but simultaneously with the alarm being raised the Sergeant was behind him.

Charged at the Central Magistracy this morning before Mr. R. E. Lindsell with committing a felony, the evidence was all against the defendant. He attempted to enlist the Magistrate's sympathy and evade punishment by shivering in Court and showing symptoms of apoplexy. His Worship deferred sentence to enable defendant's physical condition to be ascertained.
NOTABLE ADVANCES.
AMERICA ELIMINATES WASTE.
PROSPERITY OF INDUSTRY.
(Kuter's Service.)
The annual report issued by Mr. Hoover, emphasises the progress of American industries in eliminating waste.

The country has also benefited by notable advances in science and the improvement in methods of management and prohibition. Thus it has the highest real wage in its history and has had a three years remarkable price stability.
Mr. Hoover recommends a radical reduction in fees for passport and visas, the simplification of formalities in the appointment of competent officers to measure tonnage of vessels; and the uniform application of American measurement and regulations so as to prevent discrimination against American vessels, and the enactment of load-line legislation similar to that of European maritime powers.
LIVE BOMBS.

ARMS FROM THE FAR
EAST.
(Reuter's Service)

At the trial of the nine Bengalis in connection with a bomb factory, the prosecution stated that the police finds included a live bomb of the most dangerous type ever before discovered by such searches; notes on the manufacture of 72 kinds of explosives, and the finding of a document addressed to a steamer clerk indicating how arms and ammunition were being smuggled into India from Singapore and the Far East.
[A message from Calcutta on Nov. 11 said: The police have discovered a bomb factory and seized the contents. They have arrested eleven Bengalis.]

PLANES COLLIDE 8,000
FEET UP
AIRMEN KILLED.
(Router's American Services)
The naval airman, Captain Shepherd and Lieutenant Christian, were killed by planes colled in an altitude of $3,000 feet over San Diego.
SHOT HIMSELF.
SGT. BLACKMAN FOUND DEAD.
THIS MORNING'S SAD NEWS.
The sad news was received at Police Headquarters of the death of Lance-Sergeant A. H. Blackman through suicide early this morning at his quarters at Salkong Police Station in the New Territories.
A revolver with which he shot himself was found beside him, and the nature of the bullet wound points to death having been instantaneous.

No motive has been found for Sergeant Blackman thus ending his life at the early age of 28, but it is believed that he was brooding over a temporary illness and shot himself while mentally deranged. He was placed on the sick list yesterday morning suffering from fever with a temperature of 102 degrees, and the staff at the station who attended to him devotedly in what was thought to be a passing illness received a shock when he was found dead soon after the report of a revolver shot.

By his winning ways and kind disposition, the late Sergeant made many friends who will sadly miss him, while his conduct during eight years' service won the confidence and esteem of his superior officers.

Mr. Blackman joined the Hong Kong Police in 1917 and was unmarried. Prior to coming here he was in the Royal Marines and served in the war. Until a month ago when he was sent to the New Territories at his own request, he was attached to the charge room at the Water Police Station.
SHAFT DAMAGED.
“FATSHAN” RETURNS TO WHARF.

Leaving the Hongkong wharf at eight this morning with passengers for Canton, the China Navigation S.S. Co.'s "Fatshan" (run in conjunction with the Steamboat Co.) put back shortly before ten and discharged as the trip was interrupted by a damaged shaft.
The “Fatshan” was near Capsu-min when the trouble occurred and she returned on her own steam.
Repairs will be effected in dock and the steamer will rejoin the run in a few days.
SHANGHAI INQUIRY
HOUSE OF COMMONS QUESTION.
London, Dec. 2.
(Reuter's Service.)

In the House of Commons, questioned in regard to the "general conclusions of the International Judicial Commission which recently considered the Shanghai disturbances, Mr. Ronald McNeill, Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs, stated the information possessed by the Government was insufficient to enable him to reply. Further information had been requested telegraphically.
COTTON GAMBLING.
BANKRUPTCY. FOR OLDHAM FIRM

The Lancashire cotton trade has been startled by the announcement of a liquidator for the cotton mills company at Oldham. That company has lost at least £3,500,000, largely by gambling in cotton figures and actual cotton. It is proposed to form a new company to take over the present company's mills at a price of £600,000.
ST. STEPHEN'S COLLEGE.
THE LATE MR CHAU SIU-KI'S PORTRAIT.
GOVERNOR PERFORMS UNVEILING
His Excellency the Governor, Mr. Cecil Clementi, unveiled this morning at St. Stephen's College a portrait of the late Mr. ChauSiuki who was killed as a result of the Po Hing Fong disaster.

The portrait was presented to St. Stephen's College by the College Council on which the late Mr. Chau had served and in connection with whose work he had taken a keen and active interest as indeed he did in all matters appertaining to education and public welfare in Hongkong.

His Excellency was accompanied on the platform at the school hall in the temporary buildings by the warden of St. Stephen's College, the Rev. W. H. Hewitt, M.A., B.D., the Right Rev. C. R. Dup�ly, Bishop of Victoria, Sir Henry Pollock, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, Mr. G. N. Orme, director of education, the Hon. Mr. Chow Shou-son, the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall, Mr. S. W. T'so and Mr. T. N. Chow, son of Mr. Chow Siu-ki.

Bishop Duppy said that as chairman of the college council it was his privilege to welcome those present to St. Stephen's College. The Council was sorry it could only welcome the guests to temporary quarters and it hoped that the time would soon come when it would have worthy buildings in which the work of the College might be carried on. The Council was very grateful to His Excellency for sparing time to be present on the occasion when it was desired to do honour to the memory of one who not only set a very high standard of service as regarded the community generally but who had also identified himself with the work of the college.
Bishop Duppy then called on the chaplain of the College, the Rev. E. W. L. Martin, to read a chapter from the book of Ecclesians ticus and the prayer for benefactors from the College prayer book. During the prayer the assembly rose.
College Benefactor.

The Rev. W. H. Hewitt, in a short address, dwelt on the services as benefactor to St. Stephen's College of the late Mr. Chau Su-ki and referred to the manner in which he had freely spent himself in the service of the community. Referring to the willingness with which the late Mr. Chau Su-ki had advised and helped the Council and the school, Mr. Hewitt mentioned that in June he, together with the Chinese members of the Council, took the trouble to go to the college and talk to the students and masters to put before them the situation as it appeared to the older members of the Chinese community. It was largely owing to the efficiency of such advice that the students and staff at that time were able to take a sane outlook on the situation and prevent the work of the College from being interrupted.

ROSEBUD WEDDING.

BOUQUETS. AT CATHEDRAL
CEREMONY.
HANLON—DODWELL.
Very pretty bouquets of pink rosebuds were carried by the bridesmaid while the bride herself had white chrysanthemum and rosebuds at this morning's St. John's Cathedral wedding.
The contracting parties were Mr. Edwin M. Hanlon, son of Mr. and Mrs. N. Hanlon, Nottingham, England, and Miss. Fanny Dorothy Dodwell, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. W. Dodwell, Rugby, England.
The Rev. T. B. Powell, M.A., officiated.
The bride's dress was of ivory crepe-de-chine with silver lace trimmings.
Miss Frances Stevenson, the bridesmaid, wore a dress of flowered chiffon with hat to match.
Mr. W. Macfarlane gave the bride away and Mrs. W. Macfarlane was the matron of honour. Supporting the bridegroom was Mr. J. W. Blackley as "best man."
After the service, a reception was held at the residence of Mr. and Mrs. A. Macfarlane, East Point.
The bride's travelling dress was of mauve crepe-de-chine. Overnight the honeymooo will be spent at Repulse Bay and then at Tungshan, Canton.

"On my return to Hongkong I had much looked forward to meeting Mr. Chau Siu-ki again," said His Excellency, "but he has gone, like other of my friends during my twelve years' absence.—Sir Kai Ho Kai, Sir Bo San Wei Yuk. Mr. Lau Chu-pak, Mr. Fung Wachun and others, both in Hongkong and the New Territories. My return has, therefore, not only been an occasion of joy to me but also in other ways of grief.
Service to Education.

“I am very glad to day to do honour to one who was not only a very old friend but also one who has done great service to Hong Kong. His public service has already been referred to and that to education is excellently summarised in the letter which the warden of St. Stephen's College sent to my private secretary prior to my coming here.”

His Excellency then read this letter which stated that Mr. Chau Siu-ki was one of the original group of Chinese gentlemen who in 1902 approached Mr. (now Bishop) Banister, the then secretary of the C.M.S., with the request that the Society should start a school for Chinese boys. The late Sir Kai Ho Kai and Dr. S. W. T'so were associated with him in this matter. When Archdeacon Barnett was appointed Headmaster in 1908 those gentlemen and others assisted him with their help and advice. On one occasion, the late Mr. Chau Siu-ki had told him (the warden) that about 80 per cent. of the boys of the school were his relatives or sons of friends and acquaintances of his.

Other services in connection with the founding of the preparatory school which eventually became St. Stephen's Girls' College, also with the founding of the Arts Faculty were referred to. In conclusion His Excellency remarked that they did well in view of the record of services contained in Mr. Hewitt's letter to do honour to the memory of their benefactor and he wished to associate himself with their expressions of gratitude for his services.

Mr. T. N. Chau, son of the late Mr. Chau Sildi, thanked the College Council for the honour, thur had done to the memory of his father, also His Excellency for attending. The family felt that it was the highest honour that could be held to him.
PEACE MISSION.
PROJECT FOR VISIT TO CANTON
ABOUT A HUNDRED GOING.
About a hundred Hongkong Chinese propose going to Canton us a mission of observation.

Yesterday a joint meeting was held of the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, the Tung Wah Hospital, the Twenty-four Associated Guilds and the Joint Union of District Commercial Guilds at which an offer from the Canton Navigation Co. was read, offering free passages. It is hoped to obtain permission to berth the steamer alongside the wharf at Canton. This may be granted on a stipulation that cargo be not carried.
Mr. Yeung Sai-ngnam and Mr. Kan Kum-shek may travel with the party. Notice will first be sent to Canton.
As reported in yesterday's "China Mail" the party will attempt to establish cordial relations with both the Canton Government and the workers.
ANTON REPORTER

After mentioning that Hong-kong's delegates were to have gone up during the last week-end, the "Canton Gazette" quotes a letter to the Strike Executive by Wong Ching-wa (chairman of the Police Council); as follows:—

The question in regard to the despatch of delegates to negotiate with the Hongkong representatives for settling the strike was discussed at our meeting held on November 27. It was decided afterwards that three representatives should be elected by the Strike Committee and one by the Four Chambers of Commerce.

Although Mr. Yeung Sai-ngsaam has been reported as having emphasised that his visit to Hong-kong is purely personal and in a strictly private capacity, it is interesting to note that the "Canton Gazette" of Tuesday, says:—

During the period of the present strike which is being carried on, so vigorously, the intercourse with Hongkong and Macao has been absolutely cut off. Recently our Government, in order to investigate the latest conditions in Macao and Hongkong, specially appointed Yeung Sai-nguam as special delegate for the purpose. After the appointment, Mr. Yeung proceeded to Hongkong on November 29 on the 8.3. "Honam."
